title: Keeping paper and cardboard clean and dry
description: Paper fibres are fragile: one wet, greasy load can spoil a whole batch, so dry storage matters more than almost anything.

body.heading: Why water and grease are the enemies
paragraphs: Paper is recycled by pulping it back into fibres, and every round of recycling shortens those fibres. Waterlogged paper often arrives at the plant already falling apart and mouldy, and grease soaks into fibres in a way that cannot be washed out.
That is why a single soggy, food-stained box can cause a whole bundle to be rejected. The rest of the load was fine; the contamination was not.

body.heading: Simple storage habits
paragraphs: Keep the lid on the recycling bin, especially in rainy weather, and store paper indoors or under cover until collection day if your bin lives outside. Flattening boxes saves space and stops them becoming buckets that collect rain.

If cardboard gets a little damp at the edges it is usually still fine. If it is sodden, falling apart or smells of mould, it is kinder to the system to compost it at home if you can, or let it go with general waste.

body.heading: Food-stained paper
paragraphs: Clean paper plates, napkins and kitchen roll cannot be recycled once used with food, but many food-waste and compost schemes accept them, because the fibres feed soil rather than new paper.
For pizza boxes, tear off the clean lid for recycling and compost or bin the greasy base. It takes five seconds and keeps the good fibre in circulation.

takeaway: Dry, clean and flattened: treat paper gently and nearly all of it can become paper again.
